title: Restricted routes and spatial adjacency
transcript: A route follows legal connections. Two places can look close on a picture without having an edge between them. Read exactly what makes them neighbours. When paths must avoid a particular connection, look for an easy total and subtract the routes that use that connection.

In AMC grid practice, sharing a side and sharing a corner are different. Mark the legal exits before counting routes. In a Rossmoyne style route problem, the order of visits can matter even when the same stops appear. Label both the places and the route positions.
A four by three board has a marked corner cell. Two cells are neighbours only if they share a full side. How many neighbours does it have? Test the cells directly across each of the four sides.
Two sides of a corner cell touch the boundary. Across each of its other two sides there is a cell on the board. A diagonal cell touches only at a point. The marked corner has exactly two neighbours.
On a grid, start at intersection one, three and stop at two, four. Every move is one horizontal or vertical step. List the possible intermediate points on a two-step route.

Moving right then up passes through two, three. Moving up then right passes through one, four. Any other first move leaves you more than one step from the finish. There are only two legal routes in exactly two steps.

There are three red stops and three blue stops, each labelled. Every move goes between opposite colours. All those connections are open except the one joining red two and blue one. Start at red one, finish at blue three, and visit every stop exactly once. How many routes are legal?

Colours alternate. The free red stops can fill their two positions in two orders. The free blue stops have the same count. Count the forbidden routes in both directions. When red two is followed by blue one, there are one positions for the pair because the endpoints are already reserved. In the reverse order there are two positions. When either pair is placed, the other one free stops of each colour can be ordered independently.

A route contains only one red two and one blue one. Its forbidden pair has a unique orientation and position, so there are three forbidden routes. Subtract those from all alternating routes. The number of legal routes is one.

Sharing a corner does not count as sharing a full side. Apply the exact adjacency definition each time you list neighbours. A closed two-way connection is forbidden in either direction. Check both ways it could appear in the route.

Sketch the legal edges and mark the endpoint rules. Decide whether the question counts endpoints, intermediate stops or whole routes. Look for a forced pattern such as alternating colours. Count those routes before removing any restricted cases, and check you removed each once.
